## Sustainable future: challenges and opportunities of the wetland

The master plan that will guide the future of the Charca de Suárez between 2024 and 2030 outlines an ambitious horizon, where conservation and public use will have to learn to coexist without stepping on each other's toes. The roadmap approved by the Motril City Council contemplates the expansion of the protected surface area by five hectares, a decision that will make it possible to safeguard adjacent land that currently acts as a buffer zone against urban pressure from the surrounding area. That territorial gain is not a simple administrative gesture: every square meter incorporated into the wetland's perimeter reduces the risk that future buildings or infrastructure will alter water flows and the tranquility required by nesting birds.

Among the planned actions, the construction of an elevated bird observatory stands out, a structure that will completely change the visitor experience. From that vantage point, amateur ornithologists and the curious will be able to observe the lagoons without needing to approach the shores, thus avoiding trampling of marsh vegetation and disturbance to the most sensitive species. The project also includes a floating walkway over the main lagoon, a route that will allow visitors to venture into the heart of the wetland without direct contact with the bed or the plant communities that serve as refuge for wildlife. Both infrastructures respond to the same philosophy: bringing the ecosystem closer to people without that proximity becoming a threat.

The digitalization of management is another of the pillars on which the immediate future of the Charca rests. The master plan provides for the installation of water quality sensors that will measure parameters such as salinity, dissolved oxygen, or temperature in real time—variables that determine the survival of such demanding species as the Spanish toothcarp or the marbled teal. That data will make it possible to detect early any alteration in water inputs, whether due to prolonged drought, marine intrusion, or accidental spills, and to activate response protocols before the damage becomes irreversible. Surveillance cameras, for their part, will serve a dual function: deterring those who access outside opening hours or through unauthorized areas, and documenting wildlife behavior without interfering with their routines.

The main challenge facing the wetland is neither technical nor budgetary, but one of balance. The growing popularity of the Charca de Suárez as a nature destination has multiplied the number of visitors in recent years—an influx that generates educational and economic benefits, but also subjects the ecosystem to constant pressure. To manage that tension, the master plan establishes a prior reservation system and capacity limits that will regulate access during periods of highest demand, especially on weekends and during bird breeding seasons. The measure seeks to ensure that the visitor experience remains high-quality without the constant flow of people ending up driving away the very species people come to observe.

The declaration as a Special Protection Area for Birds, integrated into the European Natura 2000 network, is shaping up as the definitive boost to secure the future of the site. That recognition, which the regional administration is processing in coordination with the Motril city council, would grant the Charca a reinforced protection status that would condition any urban or agricultural project in its immediate surroundings. Beyond the legal safeguard, the SPA designation would function as a quality seal that would position the wetland in international birdwatching tourism circuits—a segment that moves millions of travelers each year willing to travel to observe birds in their natural habitats.

The financing of these actions does not start from zero. The Motril City Council has been consolidating a sustained investment line that already exceeds one and a half million euros over the last four-year period—a figure that demonstrates that the commitment to the Charca is not a passing fad. Added to that amount will be contributions from European and regional funds linked to biodiversity conservation, as well as resources generated by the interpretation center itself through guided activities and educational programs. The economic sustainability of the project is as important as the ecological one: without a management model that guarantees stable income, any future plan would remain dead on arrival.

The execution schedule extends over the next six years, with differentiated phases that will allow the impact of each intervention to be assessed before undertaking the next. That temporal prudence responds to a lesson learned in other Andalusian wetlands, where the hasty execution of public-use infrastructure caused alterations that later took years to reverse. The Charca de Suárez has the advantage of arriving late to that process: it can observe the mistakes of others and apply already proven solutions, adapting them to the particularities of a small coastal wetland where every decision has immediate consequences.

The future of the Charca is also played out on the ground of public perception. A wetland that the local population feels is their own is a defended wetland, and that is why the master plan reserves a prominent role for environmental education and neighborhood participation. School visits, volunteer programs, and scientific bird-ringing days are not complementary activities, but central pieces of a strategy that seeks to create a broad and committed social base. That network of alliances becomes essential when tensions arise with other land uses, such as intensive agriculture or urban development, which have historically pressured the natural areas of the Granada coast.

The expansion of the protected surface area, the improvement of observation infrastructure, and the digitalization of management paint a promising scenario, but the true success of the plan will be measured in biological indicators. The stable presence of threatened species, the increase in nesting populations, and the recovery of native flora will be the tests that determine whether the investments have served for something more than beautifying a natural space. The Charca de Suárez faces the challenge of growing without becoming denatured, of opening to the public without becoming a theme park, of modernizing without losing the wild character that made it valuable. That balance, as difficult to achieve as to maintain, will mark the difference between a wetland that survives and a wetland that thrives.
